We prove that (i) any non-adaptive policy suffers linear regret after a preference shift, (ii) no fixed exploration rate achieves low regret in both stationary and non-stationary regimes, and (iii) PEARL's cumulative regret scales with the number of shifted users N_s, not the total population N. On PRISM, a personalized LLM response selection benchmark (1,500 users, 21 LLMs), PEARL beats greedy by +4.0 points and the best neural bandit baseline by +2.5 points (p<0.001), while performing on par with greedy when preferences are stable. It beats sliding-window and discounted approaches by 3 to 10 points, showing that selective forgetting outperforms uniform forgetting. The selection policy is a ~100K-parameter MLP that runs in milliseconds on CPU, leaves LLM weights frozen, and works with any API-based model.

papers.title: Vision Paper: Why Distributed LLM Post-Training and Decentralized Alignment Are Now Essential
papers.abstract: This vision paper argues that distributed learning, including federated and decentralized, should become a first-class paradigm in LLM post-training, not merely a privacy add-on. Current methods like RLHF and DPO rest on an invisible assumption: preference data should be centralized. We contend this assumption is scientifically unjustified, practically unsustainable, and ethically problematic. As LLMs deploy into healthcare, law, finance, and multilingual communities, preference data originates from populations that cannot or will not centralize. We develop a three-pillar argument grounded in (1) privacy and data sovereignty, (2) pluralism and representational equity, and (3) robustness and scalability. We formalize key technical challenges unique to this intersection, reference drift, preference heterogeneity, and the DP-utility trade-off for contrastive losses, and propose concrete algorithmic directions, and sketch a research agenda. Our analysis shows distributed post-training is not only necessary but tractable, and ignoring it risks AI that is legally noncompliant, representationally narrow, and brittle at scale.

papers.title: Interplay between Spin Stripes and Pairing Crossover in the Bilayer Hubbard Model
papers.abstract: Whether $d$-wave or $s_\pm$-wave pairing prevails in the bilayer nickelate \ce{La3Ni2O7} remains unresolved, and how its observed spin order and magnetic excitations relate to the pairing mechanism is unclear. Here, we use finite-temperature determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a minimal bilayer Hubbard model to investigate pairing competition at strong interlayer coupling, where intralayer and interlayer antiferromagnetic correlations have comparable strengths. We find that spin stripes develop spontaneously with increasing hole doping, accompanied by a crossover of the dominant pairing symmetry from $d$-wave to $s_\pm$-wave. The crossover tracks the changing relative strengths of the spin correlations, with the interlayer correlations overtaking their intralayer counterparts in magnitude. Concomitantly, the dynamical spin structure factor exhibits a momentum-dependent reorganization of the magnetic excitations, consistent with fluctuating spin stripes. Our results identify the structure of spin fluctuations as a key link between spin stripes and pairing competition, offering a minimal-model perspective for understanding \ce{La3Ni2O7}.

papers.title: RACE: Calibrated Cumulative Scoring for Rollout-Free Robot Policy Checkpoint Selection
papers.abstract: Assessing the deployment performance of learned robot policies during training is challenging, as directly measuring task success requires costly real-world trials for each candidate checkpoint. Averaged validation loss offers a rollout-free alternative, but its checkpoint rankings can be inconsistent with deployment performance. We analyze two limitations of this criterion: it penalizes action deviations without considering whether the policy can recover from them, and gives later reference predictions equal weight even when earlier deviations may lead execution away from the reference. We propose RACE, a novel rollout-free metric for ranking checkpoints using a fixed set of held-out successful trajectories. RACE calibrates action deviations against state-conditional thresholds derived from action differences at similar states in these trajectories. We aggregate these scores through a running product, so that a substantial deviation reduces the contribution of subsequent reference predictions. Averaging the resulting cumulative scores over time and across trajectories yields the checkpoint score. In simulation, RACE outperforms baselines across validation sources, while several baselines degrade sharply when the validation set changes. On real robots, its rankings align with deployment success across the evaluated policy backbones and tasks of varying difficulty. Perturbation analyses further show that RACE distinguishes deviations with markedly different effects on task success, even when baselines respond similarly.

papers.title: Ferroelectricity and Peierls transition in MOI$_2$ (M=Ta, Nb): a first-principle analysis
papers.abstract: The van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI$_2$ hosts a polar distortion that is commonly attributed to the Peierls dimerization of its Nb chains. Here we show, using first-principles calculations and a Landau-type energy, that the polar instability is in fact a distinct order parameter that does not stem from the Peierls mode condensation and that three main distinct modes are important in the whole MOI$_2$ family. They are a polar mode $P$, an antipolar mode $η$, and a Peierls mode $δ$, whose stabilities and couplings strongly depend on the nature of the $M$ metal element, as evidenced by the fact that the isostructural, TaOI$_2$ system is not polar while possessing Peirls distortions.

papers.title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
papers.abstract: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

papers.title: Functional inequalities from the fundamental limits of Bayesian estimation
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian information-theoretic framework for proving functional inequalities for log-concave measures. Motivated by Klartag and Ordentlich, we establish a unified equivalence between $Φ$-Sobolev inequalities and Bayesian estimation lower bounds: for a large class of smooth convex $Φ$, a log-concave measure $μ$ satisfies a $Φ$-Sobolev inequality with constant $C>0$ if and only if for $X\simμ$, any $t>0$, and any real-valued measurable $f$, the Bayes risk of estimating $f(X)$ under the $Φ$-Bregman loss from the Gaussian additive observation $Y_t=\sqrt tX+G, G\sim N(0,I_n)$ is at least a $1/(1+Ct)$-fraction of that of the trivial estimator. Combining it with direct information-theoretic arguments, such as testing-to-estimation reductions, we obtain old and new functional inequalities: - For the Poincaré inequality, corresponding to $Φ(x)=(x-1)^2$, we give a simple static information-theoretic proof that the Poincaré constant of an isotropic log-concave measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $O(n^{1/2})$, first proven via stochastic localization in the seminal work of Lee and Vempala. - For the log-Sobolev inequality, corresponding to $Φ(x)=x\log x$, we prove that all smooth $K$-subgaussian log-concave measures $μ$ satisfy $C_{\mathrm{LS}}(μ)\lesssim K^2n^{1/4}$, surpassing the recent state-of-the-art bound of $O(K^2n^{1/2})$ by Bizeul. In parallel and independent work, OpenAI claimed the optimal bound $O(K^2)$ in their October 6, 2026 release of 722 papers. - Finally, we give a Bayesian reformulation of the common structure of the three recent proofs of the Kannan--Lovász--Simonovits conjecture, a dimension-free Poincaré bound for isotropic log-concave measures [BK26; BKL26; SZ26]. Tools from the study of the "low-degree MMSE" in computational complexity of statistical inference motivate and recast key steps and quantities of these proofs.

papers.title: Variational exponential estimates and stationary large deviations for SPDEs
papers.abstract: We establish an abstract criterion for large deviations of invariant measures when the deterministic dynamics has a single globally attracting equilibrium. Deterministic regularisation and attraction yield an endpoint estimate for long controlled paths of bounded action, uniformly over each fixed bounded initial set. This allows the finite time Freidlin-Wentzell uniform LDP on bounded initial sets to be combined directly with stationary exponential norm estimates. The proof requires neither a separate exponential tightness argument nor a Dembo-Zeitouni uniform LDP, and imposes no decay condition on differences between controlled trajectories. Finite path approximation identifies the quasipotential as the good rate function. We also establish a variational criterion based on the Boué-Dupuis representation that derives exponential estimates from bounds for controlled outputs, without requiring their convergence. Uniform controlled terminal moments yield estimates uniform in time, which pass to Krylov-Bogoliubov invariant measures. Together, these results establish stationary LDPs in four regimes: two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with possibly unbounded, globally Lipschitz, uniformly positive scalar amplitudes and vanishing noise correlation; reaction-diffusion systems without the additional restriction linking noise growth to reaction strength; Allen-Cahn equations with opposite boundary values and globally Lipschitz, uniformly nondegenerate multiplicative space-time white noise on intervals of arbitrary length; and Burgers equations with fixed covariance $(-Δ)^α$, $0\leqα<1/2$. For Burgers, we also obtain Gaussian norm estimates.

papers.title: Autonomy and Coordination in Intelligent Manufacturing: A Recursive Autonomous Agent Framework
papers.abstract: Intelligent production requires systems to make decisions and organize work according to production goals and operating conditions. It also requires continuous adjustment through feedback. This paper analyzes intelligence in human production organizations from a complex adaptive systems (CAS) perspective. The analysis identifies two coupled mechanisms: individual autonomy and collective coordination. Individual autonomy enables actors to form local decisions using available information. Collective coordination aligns these decisions with shared goals and joint constraints. Learning and adaptation improve both mechanisms over time. A production-system model formalizes how local decision rules and coordination jointly form system decisions. On this basis, we propose the Recursive Autonomous Agent (RAA) framework, which combines goal-driven autonomous agents with a recursive organizational structure. Goal contracts define local objectives and operating boundaries, while capability contracts support the selection and composition of production units. Common interfaces allow coordinated groups to participate as units in larger organizations, connecting equipment, production lines, and factories. RAA thus provides an engineering approach to next-generation intelligent manufacturing, translating the requirements of intelligence, openness, and system-wide integration into mechanisms for autonomous and coordinated production.

papers.title: Classical records and Bell correlations in a dynamically formed quantum body
papers.abstract: Competing quantum contacts can create a boundary that was absent from the specification of a subsystem. We construct approximately isolated bodies from bare field vacuum and zero-centred contact packets. A binding contribution with vanishing mean energy density nevertheless changes a bounded formation signal by order one at the same clock. On the formed material spins and their original memories, coarse collective records precede an all-outcome Bell violation. The field evolves dynamically, with the finite bath, residual boundary interaction, failed records and preparation costs retained. The result connects dynamical subsystem formation, classical collective records and microscopic nonlocality, with polynomial resources in the stated preparation and measurement class.

papers.title: A Hybrid Approach for Automated Security Pattern Recovery
papers.abstract: Security-by-design emphasises integrating security into software design and development. Security pattern catalogues operationalise this principle by prescribing reusable architectural solutions to recurring security problems. However, recovering their implementations from source code remains challenging because security patterns are abstract, span multiple components, and admit many valid implementations. We present SecPatRec, a hybrid approach for automated security pattern recovery from source code repositories. We treat a security pattern as a reference architecture and frame its recovery as a deductive task: determining which prescribed roles are present, grounding them in code entities, and recovering their interaction sequences. SecPatRec pairs a ReAct-style LLM agent equipped with semantic and lexical code search for role detection and grounding with static code property graph analysis for interaction recovery. We curate a human-validated ground-truth dataset of 100 pattern instances covering five security patterns across 93 open-source Java and Python repositories, and introduce a three-level evaluation framework measuring recovery correctness against this ground truth. We evaluate SecPatRec using four LLMs, including proprietary and open-source models. Averaged over all models and pattern instances, SecPatRec achieves role-detection accuracy of 0.84, role-grounding similarity of 0.84, and an interaction-recovery score of 0.66. Compared to a one-shot end-to-end LLM baseline, SecPatRec achieves higher aggregate recovery scores and lower estimated LLM API costs per run, while processing repositories that exceed the baseline's configured input limit. The recovered role mappings and statically derived interaction sequences provide structural and behavioural evidence that can support inspection of security-pattern implementations.

papers.title: A geometric proof of multivariate self-normalized moderate deviations via ridge regularization
papers.abstract: Let $X,X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d.\ random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $d\ge1$ is fixed. Assume that $\mathbb{E} X=0$, $\mathbb{E} XX^\top=I_d$ and $\mathbb{E}\|X\|^3<\infty$. We prove a Cramér type moderate deviation theorem for a multivariate self-normalized radius statistic, that is, for every $a_n=o(n^{1/6})$, \[ \sup_{0\le x\le a_n} \left|\frac{\mathbb{P}(U_{n,+}\ge x)}{\mathbb{P}(χ_d\ge x)}-1\right|\to0, \] where $χ_d$ is the Euclidean norm of a standard normal vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and \[ U_{n,+}^2=S_n^\top A_n^+S_n, \qquad S_n=\sum_{j=1}^nX_j, \qquad A_n=\sum_{j=1}^nX_jX_j^\top. \] Here $A_n^+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose inverse. We further prove that the same result holds for the corresponding Hotelling $T^2$ statistic. This work closes the moment gap between the previously known finite $(3+δ)$ moment condition for Hotelling moderate deviations and the finite third moment boundary. Our proof adopts a geometric approach. Truncation at the finite-third-moment scale yields a truncated covariance matrix whose concentration error is negligible relative to the target \(χ_d\) tail. Uniform projected self-normalized moderate deviations are then averaged over directions and, after a whitening map with a ridge term, become a spherical cap transform of the radial distribution. A local Abel inversion recovers the radial tail, and deterministic comparison removes the ridge and the truncation.

papers.title: Analytic two-body density-matrix spectrum of the Fermionic Tonks-Girardeau gas
papers.abstract: The two-body density matrix (TBDM) of a quantum many-body system provides information about particle correlations, e.g., pairing. In this work, we derive the complete spectrum of the TBDM of the fermionic Tonks-Girardeau gas using its exact ground-state wavefunction in second quantization. We obtain analytical expressions for all eigenvalues and eigenvectors for an arbitrary number of particles and identify two different types of eigenstates: collective states, formed by superpositions of paired momentum modes, and single-determinant states. We provide a physical interpretation of this structure, explaining the origin of the different eigenstates and their degeneracies. We further derive an asymptotic expansion for the largest eigenvalue, improving on previous estimates and analytically confirming its linear scaling with the particle number, thereby indicating off-diagonal long-range order. For the high-index collective states, we obtain simpler expressions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, showing that the eigenvalues decay as $n^{-4}$ and that the eigenvectors become independent of the number of particles. Finally, we discuss the connection between the collective states and an effective description in terms of composite bosons, whose spectral properties suggest a behavior consistent with Tan's contact for interacting bosonic systems.

papers.title: Hybrid Hadrons: Origins and Development
papers.abstract: Hybrid hadrons are states in which the gluonic field of the strong force contributes to the structure of the hadron. The idea arose in several places at nearly the same time in the mid-1970s because the advent of quantum chromodynamics made it clear that the carriers of the strong force are dynamical degrees of freedom. This resulted in the cavity resonators of the MIT bag model, in the vibrating strings inherited from the dual resonance model, in the Budapest membrane bag, and in a constituent-gluon potential model. The idea was subsequently developed in the early 1980s into a phenomenology capable of predicting masses, quantum numbers, and decay signatures. This article traces that history from the primary literature, giving close attention to dates of submission and to who first proposed what, and supplements the written record with recollections of many of the principal participants. It closes by surveying the current state of experimental, theoretical, and lattice research.

papers.title: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid Feasibility and Manipulation Resistance in Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading
papers.abstract: Blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy markets let neighbors trade directly, but concentrate unchecked power in the clearing operator. Most prior work addresses only part of this: network-aware clearing respects grid constraints but operates on plaintext allocations, while privacy-preserving designs hide bids yet either drop the network constraint, enforce it only inside an unauditable computation, or recover it at the cost of a per-circuit trusted setup. Neither considers what happens if an adversary captures the operator's clearing privilege to reorder trades for profit or curtail a rival. We present GRIDSHIELD, a P2P energy-trading system that clears sealed bids with an order-independent batch program, removing the welfare a compromised operator can extract by reordering trades, and proves the result grid-feasible via an aggregated congestion-feasibility proof (ACFP). Exploiting the additive homomorphism of Pedersen commitments, ACFP reconstructs each grid constraint directly from per-bus commitments, reducing feeder-wide feasibility verification over any public grid constraints to a single aggregated range proof over the hidden allocation, with a reveal-and-recompute challenge that catches feasible yet unfair clearings. We introduce congestion-responsibility fairness (CRF), a metric scoring curtailment against each party's physical responsibility for congestion rather than consumption. We evaluate GRIDSHIELD against three prior P2P energy-trading designs across four feeders, including a 240-node Midwest feeder with real hourly loads, on a live Hyperledger Fabric network benchmarked with Hyperledger Caliper. GRIDSHIELD proves an entire round feasible with a few-kilobyte proof and no trusted setup, rejects infeasible allocations two of the three compared designs accept, and sustains $\approx$1064 tx/s.

papers.title: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly automate complex tasks, but human decision capacity does not scale with their capabilities. In many applications, humans remain essential for providing private context, authority, or judgments unavailable to the agent. We formulate human decision capacity allocation: given multiple consultation opportunities and a limited budget, at which decisions should an LLM agent consult a human? The central challenge is estimating consultation value, which is executor-dependent because the same human input may benefit different downstream agents differently. We introduce Consultation Value Distillation (CVD), which estimates consultation values offline using Monte Carlo executor rollouts and distills these values into lightweight predictors for budgeted allocation, requiring no rollout-based value estimation at deployment. Across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors, CVD improves allocation through joint and continuation-aware value learning, while independent consultation values remain competitive in several settings. CVD also broadly outperforms direct prompting and Value of Information where applicable, remains robust with substantially less rollout supervision, and enables nearly lossless approximate allocation at low search cost.

papers.title: Towards the Query Complexity of Sampling under Strong Log-Concavity and Log-Sobolev Inequalities
papers.abstract: We study the query complexity of sampling from smooth distributions on $\mathbb R^d$ using first-order oracles. For $d$-dimensional strongly log-concave targets with condition number $κ=2$, we prove that any randomized sampler requires $\exp({Ω(\log^{1/3} d)})$ queries even from a constant warm start. This rules out polylogarithmic dimension dependence and strictly separates strongly log-concave sampling from Gaussian sampling. For targets with $L$-smooth potentials satisfying an $α$-log-Sobolev inequality with $κ= L/α$, we prove an $Ω(κ)$ query lower bound for $d\gtrsim\log^2κ$. This shows that log-Sobolev sampling is strictly harder than strongly log-concave sampling. Our proofs construct instance-dependent tests that target samples typically pass but outputs of algorithms making few queries typically fail. For strongly log-concave targets, we embed a sequence of hidden Gaussian into high-degree tensor polynomial with smooth gates, forcing any algorithm to uncover the layers sequentially. The log-Sobolev construction hides a constant fraction of the target mass in angular caps while controlling the log-Sobolev constant via delicate estimates.

papers.title: Uncertainty aware prediction from incomplete clinical records: a conformal prediction study of Parkinsonian classification using C-OPN data
papers.abstract: Background: Incomplete clinical records and imbalanced diagnostic groups complicate Parkinsonian classification. We examined whether incomplete records could support useful lists of diagnostic possibilities through conformal prediction, assessing how often the lists retained the recorded diagnosis, their length and the uncertainty remaining. Methods: We analyzed records from 3,434 Canadian Open Parkinson Network participants: 2,853 with Parkinson's disease, 171 in the atypical Parkinsonian group (AP) and 410 healthy controls. In three repeats of five-fold cross-validation, we compared single-category predictions, conformal prediction sets and lists combined across 21 analyses using alternative models and assumptions about missing entries. An information deficit score summarized unavailable information. Results: The median proportion of eligible predictor entries unrecorded per participant was 75.6%. Single-category prediction correctly classified 89.29% of test records (balanced accuracy 55.40%), but only 10.33% of AP records. Conformal prediction sets included the recorded category in 93.35% of evaluation records and averaged 1.846 categories; combined lists increased inclusion to approximately 99% and averaged 2.289 categories. AP inclusion increased from 98.05% to 100%. Combined lists averaged 1.010 more categories in the group with the greatest information deficit than in the group with the least (95% interval 0.996-1.023). Conclusions: Even with extensive missing information and imbalanced diagnostic groups, clinical records can support informative prediction when uncertainty is quantified and expressed through sets of possible diagnoses rather than a single label. Joint assessment of list length and information deficit showed both the narrowing achieved and the records for which all three categories remained open.
authors: for the Canadian Open Parkinson Network

papers.title: Atomic-Scale Phonon Engineering for Enhanced Thermal Transport in Wafer-Scale-Bonded $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$/SiC Heterostructures
papers.abstract: Bonding semiconductors to substrates with high thermal conductivity is a promising way to solve the heat-dissipation problem of materials that transport heat poorly, and it avoids the lattice-matching constraints of conventional epitaxy. However, the lattice mismatch remains, leaving the two materials with mismatched phonon states, while poor interface quality scatters phonons even more. Together, these effects block phonon transport across the bonded interface and make interfacial thermal resistance a critical bottleneck, calling for careful interface engineering. Here, $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$/SiC serves as a model system for a phonon-bridging strategy. A nanoscale crystalline Si interlayer is designed and fabricated by wafer bonding to bridge the mismatched phonon states of $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$ and SiC. Spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations show that this Si layer opens new channels for phonon transport across the interface. The engineered interface raises the interfacial thermal conductance to 165 MW m$^{-2}$ K$^{-1}$ -- the highest value yet reported for $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$/SiC interfaces. These results offer an effective way to manage heat in $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$ devices and point to a general approach for building phonon-bridging interfaces that improve heat dissipation in heterogeneous systems.

papers.title: On rational curves relative to a divisor
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety and $D$ a reduced simple normal crossings divisor. We prove that, given a complete curve of negative $(K_X+D)$-degree, through its general points there is a rational curve whose normalization meets $D$ in at most one point. The proof uses ordinary weighted jets of a smooth family constructed from $(X,D)$, a positive parameter line bundle, and an intersection calculation on a ruled surface. We obtain an explicit degree bound depending on a projective embedding. We apply this construction to a cyclic cover compactification associated with a smooth Campana orbifold $(X,\sum_i(1-1/m_i)D_i)$. If its anticanonical divisor is big, we show that there is a covering family of free divisible Campana rational curves with fixed numerical class and contact data. In Picard number one case, the orbifold is Campana rationally connected.

papers.title: A Laplace-Transform Green's Function for Two-Zone Diffusion with Energy Losses: Application to the Geminga Pulsar Halo
papers.abstract: Extended TeV gamma-ray halos around pulsars are commonly interpreted as evidence for slow diffusion of high-energy electrons and positrons near their sources, with diffusion coefficients about two orders of magnitude below the Galactic average inferred from B/C measurements. A two-zone diffusion picture offers a natural phenomenological resolution: particles are temporarily confined in a slow-diffusion region around the source and subsequently propagate through the outer region with a diffusion coefficient close to the Galactic average. Using a Laplace-transform method, we derive an analytical Green's-function solution to the spherically symmetric two-zone diffusion equation, in which the diffusion coefficient changes discontinuously at r_b. The solution satisfies continuity of both the particle density and the diffusive flux at the boundary and reduces to the standard Gaussian kernel in the one-zone limit. For the parameter set used in our comparison, the spatial kernel and the positron flux at Earth agree numerically with an independent integral solution of the same two-zone problem. Applied to Geminga, the two-zone models examined here produce a more extended outer particle distribution and broader positron spectra than the homogeneous diffusion model, with higher positron fluxes in the TeV range. The adopted injection model further affects the height and shape of the high-energy spectral peak. The predicted gamma-ray surface-brightness profile also reproduces the main radial decline observed by HAWC.

papers.title: When File Ingestion Misleads Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Divergences in Office Documents
papers.abstract: Office documents are now routinely uploaded to large language models (LLMs) for processing. However, an LLM does not always see what a human sees, because it typically reads the text that an extractor produces from the document's underlying Office Open XML (OOXML) files. Depending on the implementation, extractors differ in which OOXML parts they read and how they interpret them, so their output can differ from what Office applications display. For example, by slightly shifting the positions of text boxes on a slide, an adversary can swap the order in which the model reads them while the slide looks unchanged. We show that this extraction divergence is an attack surface for LLM applications. In this work, we first measure what an adversary can exploit by analyzing the widely used extractors that LLM applications rely on. By combining static source code analysis with dynamic analysis, we identify 19 OOXML channels where extractors read content a human cannot see and 12 where they drop content a human can. We also find that widely used extractors ignore display formatting and reading order, so even visible content reaches the model in a different form. Building on these findings, we construct five attacks that lead the model to interpret a document differently from a human reviewer, without injecting any instruction. We test the attacks on four major chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and four coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot CLI), and every one of them is misled by at least one attack. Finally, we propose Prism, a lightweight defense that reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification before passing the text to the model. Prism also generalizes to unseen attack payloads.

papers.title: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation
papers.abstract: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.

papers.title: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles
papers.abstract: Recent LLM-centric advances can generate attractive furnished rooms by selecting and arranging assets. Yet evaluation remains limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, failing to reflect overall scene quality. To address this pressing need, we introduce GREP. Its core is a focus shift from defining specific questions to establishing a three-tier evaluation philosophy: basic physical validity checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints; visual coherence concerns compatibility in object scale, style, and composition; and, at the highest level, human-use logic requires object arrangements to align with everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent autonomously and adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. This supports scene-specific issue discovery and reliable judgments. Experiments show that (1) GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. (2) GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. (3) GREP suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. Stronger models are therefore expected not only to plan well, but also to adapt to external guidance and constraints more flexibly. Project page: https://han-808.github.io/GREP/

papers.title: WayPOP: A Panoramic Open-Set Panoptic Tracking Benchmark
papers.abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.

papers.title: Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy with entangled photons and visible-light detection
papers.abstract: Time-resolved infrared (TR-IR) spectroscopy reveals molecular structural changes and charge-carrier dynamics on their intrinsic timescales, in photosynthesis, catalysis and optoelectronic materials, but requires complex sources of ultrashort infrared pulses, cryogenically cooled detectors to overcome thermal background, and intense probes that can perturb the sample. Quantum infrared spectroscopy avoids these constraints: harnessing quantum interference between the generation processes of frequency-entangled photon pairs, it reads out the infrared response of a sample by detecting only the visible partner photon, for which efficient detectors exist. To date, it has been limited to steady-state measurements. Here we demonstrate its ultrafast, time-resolved form with a picosecond visible pump pulse and a silicon detector. Each visible pulse generates photon pairs within a picosecond window; the infrared photon of a pair probes the excited sample at a set delay after excitation, and the transient response is read out from the count rate of its visible partner. We resolve picosecond carrier dynamics in a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror near 1529 nm with a picowatt-level probe, unaffected by thermal background and by sample IR photoluminescence 50 times stronger than the probe. The approach is applicable to the mid-infrared, fingerprint region, where infrared detection is hardest, and to the terahertz region.

papers.title: Item Representations Matter: Bridging Hard Semantic IDs and Soft Prototype Mixtures for Generative Retrieval
papers.abstract: Modern recommender systems rely on generative retrieval techniques to predict the next item either as discrete codes or as a continuous vector. On the one hand, Semantic IDs (SIDs) give discrete models shared parameters and pretrained semantic structure, but discretizing items into hard codes discards some information from the original content embeddings. On the other hand, continuous models avoid quantization, yet typically use flat item lookup tables with no explicit parameter tying across items. We ask whether a continuous recommender can introduce shared structure without making it a discrete bottleneck. We propose CAP-Mix, a flow recommender that represents each item as a soft mixture of shared prototypes plus an item-specific vector. The assignments, prototypes, and item vectors are trained jointly, and the soft representation is retained at inference. Pretrained information is optional: SID responsibilities can serve as a prior over assignments, while a full content embedding can initialize the item-specific vector without changing the initial flat table. In matched comparisons on three datasets, CAP-Mix improves over a flat table on the two sparse Amazon datasets and yields a small gain on Steam when trained without pretrained information. Given only an offline SID, it outperforms a hard table built from the same tokenizer by 4.45-14.90% in HR@5. Given the full content embedding, it matches or improves a strong flat table while hard assignments regress on the sparse Amazon datasets. Overall, averaged across six benchmarks, CAP-Mix improves HR@5 and NDCG@5 by 6.9% and 13.6% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each dataset and metric, while delivering 1.4-161x the inference throughput of the discrete baselines in our experiments.

papers.title: Consistency Is Not Understanding: Orbit Audits for Neural Field Weight Readers
papers.abstract: Recognizing visual content from neural-network weights requires separating functional information from arbitrary parameter coordinates. We audit this separation with hidden-neuron permutations and positive ReLU rescalings that preserve the represented function. The study contains 480 independently fitted shape fields and 1,000 MNIST fields, with transformed copies grouped by origin. On shape recognition, a statistics reader falls from \ShapeRawStats\% to \ShapeJointStats\% accuracy under joint transformations; a normalized set reader retains \ShapeNormSet\% with unchanged predictions. Four small frozen language models obtain \LMRange\% raw accuracy with next-token scoring. A separate four-configuration reasoning experiment with 1,920 scored sessions obtains \FrontRawRange\% raw accuracy with generated answers, while fresh identical raw prompts disagree on \FrontRawRepeatRange\% of origins. Canonicalization makes equivalent prompts identical, but this neither establishes recognition nor guarantees identical generated responses. Joint correctness/agreement metrics, semantic-cue controls, fresh repeats, and exact-rational rounding bounds separate these failure modes. The result is an inspectable evaluation protocol for visual weight readers, with claims restricted to the tested fields, prompts, and execution configurations.

papers.title: DARE: Difficulty Analysis for Repair Enhancement
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents are primarily evaluated by their solve rates. However, this metric does not reveal how difficult the solved tasks are or account for differences intask difficulty across benchmarks. Determining the difficulty of individual tasks by repeatedly running multiple agents is costly, while a predicted difficulty score alone provides limited guidance on what support an agent needs. To address these challenges, we propose DARE (Difficulty Analysis for Repair Enhancement), which integrates repair-task difficulty measurement, prediction, feature-group contribution analysis, and task-specific repair support. We define continuous task difficulty as the observed failure rate across multiple coding agents. The DARE difficulty model predicts this difficulty using 151 static features extracted from benchmark artifacts. The framework also analyzes the contributions of seven Repair-Task Feature Groups to identify the characteristics most salient to each task and uses this information to select task-specific agent support. We evaluate DARE on four benchmark partitions comprising 2,594 tasks. The difficulty model's aligned predictions achieve Spearman's $ρ$ = .476-.621 on held-out partitions, and the most salient Feature Groups vary across tasks and benchmarks. Furthermore, coding-agent experiments show improved repair success when support is matched to each task's salient Feature Group. These findings demonstrate that difficulty prediction and interpretation can lead to practical improvements in automated program repair (APR), while also providing a basis for difficulty-stratified agent evaluation, cross-benchmark comparisons, and identifying areas of repair capability that warrant further improvement.

papers.title: Near linear mixing of random-cluster Glauber dynamics on random regular graphs
papers.abstract: We study the random-cluster model on locally treelike graphs at low temperatures. This is a model of dependent percolation parametrized by an edge probability $p \in (0,1)$ and a clustering weight $q \in [1,\infty)$, generalizing independent Bernoulli percolation ($q=1$) and closely related to the classical ferromagnetic Ising and Potts spin systems at integer $q$. For $q>2$, at parameter $p$ below the tree uniqueness threshold $p_{\mathsf u}(q,d)$, it is expected that sampling is easy and local Markov chains mix rapidly on all graphs with degree bounded by $d$. On typical graphs, the same is predicted at $p>p_{\mathsf s}(q,d)$, where $p_{\mathsf s}(q,d)$ is a second uniqueness transition point on the $d$-regular wired tree. Our result confirms this prediction for random regular graphs, showing that the random-cluster Glauber dynamics mix in time $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ on a random $d$-regular graph for all fixed $q>2$ and $p>p_{\mathsf s}$. For comparison, the best prior sampling results for these models that held for all $p>p_{\mathsf s}$ required $q\gtrsim \log d$ \cite{BGPZ26}. The key difficulty is that simply utilizing the contraction of cavity messages on $d$-regular trees does not suffice to cover the entire regime $q>2$. To address this issue, motivated by \cite{LS26}, we develop a careful bootstrap argument to show the shrinkage of disagreement under grand coupling. The core ideas of the proof were generated using GPT-6 and the Pharos system; the proof was then refined and simplified by the author.

papers.title: ZipDrift: Generating Multimodal Short-Horizon MPC Costs with One-Step Drifting Models
papers.abstract: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, 53% of contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, whereas an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget in 2.0%.

papers.title: Structural Lower Bounds for Quantum Property Estimation with Persistent Memory
papers.abstract: In quantum property estimation, an experimenter estimates $\operatorname{Tr}(Oρ)$ for a family of observables from independent copies of an unknown state $ρ$ simultaneously to additive error $ε$. While quantum memory can dramatically reduce sample complexity, understanding the power of a modest register that remains coherent throughout an adaptive experiment has remained an open challenge because existing frameworks require optimizing over the infinite space of measurement trees. We overcome this barrier by developing a backward-induction framework based on operator resolvents. Rather than tracking path-dependent memory states across rounds, resolvent regularization cancels internal memory trajectories exactly, reducing the lower bound to an algebraic certificate computed directly from the target observables with sharp $Ω(1/ε^2)$ scaling. Our structural rule charges only the retained dimension $K$ under arbitrary adaptive instruments and unrestricted memory lifetime. Via symmetry reductions, it yields polynomial-size linear programs that establish the optimal linear $Ω(D/(Kε^2))$ trade-off for the $D^2-1$ Paulis, eliminating the cubic loss in prior bounds. For growing weight-$w$ Pauli strings ($w=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) and quadratic Majorana cross-correlations, it proves lower bounds of $Ω(3^w/ε^2)$ and $Ω(n^2/(ε^2(1+\ln n)^2))$ against an indefinitely persistent memory of dimension $K=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. These bounds match memoryless or commuting estimators within polylogarithmic factors, demonstrating that rank constraints on the persistent register fundamentally throttle observable overlap and prevent a modest coherent memory from overcoming the sample complexity barrier.

papers.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.

papers.title: Unsupervised Neural Operators for Rotating Relativistic Stars: High-Fidelity Equation of State Inference and Pulsar Spin Evolution at Scale
papers.abstract: Observed populations of rotating neutron stars~(NSs) with millisecond-order periods are powerful probes of fundamental physics. Mass-radius measurements inform poorly constrained properties of degenerate nuclear matter, whereas high-fidelity population synthesis connects unknowns in NS formation and binary evolution to large radio-timing surveys. However, repeated structure calculations are prohibitive due to the computational cost of solving the highly coupled partial differential equations of axisymmetric general relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium that govern rotating NS interiors. Non-rotating calculations or approximate rotational corrections can bias equation of state inference and limit the fidelity of population synthesis in tracing the evolutionary history of progenitors and propagating equation of state uncertainties. In this \textit{Letter}, we develop physics-informed neural operators that can solve the axisymmetric problem with high accuracy and negligible computational cost. \textit{Our solvers are trained in a fully unsupervised setting, with the training objective informed solely by the partial differential equations, and achieve a $10^3\times$ speed-up with negligible accuracy loss}. These solvers enable scalable EoS inference that self-consistently accounts for rotation and repeated stellar-structure calculations during binary evolution, making spin predictions that account for rotational structure and EoS uncertainties computationally accessible to population synthesis.

papers.title: Gluon and Faddeev--Popov ghost propagators in rotating background: An eigenfunction approach
papers.abstract: We construct the free gluon and Faddeev--Popov ghost propagators in rigidly rotating cylindrical coordinates using an eigenfunction approach within the Feynman gauge. Starting from the quadratic gauge-fixed QCD action, we derive the corresponding kinetic operators and obtain their spectral representations. For the gluon field, a circular polarization basis diagonalizes the vector wave operator, leading to polarization-dependent shifts in the orders of the radial Bessel functions. In the absence of radial boundaries, we explicitly recover the standard Minkowski propagator in inertial Cartesian coordinates, showing that the off-diagonal tensor components in the cylindrical basis have a geometrical origin. We then extend the construction to a finite-radius cylinder satisfying the causality condition $|Ω|R<1$, imposing relative boundary conditions on the gluon field and Dirichlet conditions on the ghosts. The resulting discrete transverse spectra involve both Dirichlet and Neumann eigenvalues for the gluon modes, from which we obtain explicit spectral representations of the propagators. Our results provide a consistent framework for perturbative QCD calculations in rotating geometries, retaining the angular-momentum, polarization, and boundary effects relevant to future studies of correlation functions and radiative corrections.

papers.title: Partially Massless Condensates and Reentrant NUT/Bolt Phase Transitions in Conformal Gravity
papers.abstract: We study non-Einstein Bach-flat Taub-NUT/Bolt instantons with weakened AdS boundary conditions. In particular, the next-to-leading-order coefficient in the Fefferman--Graham expansion is nonvanishing, and it sources the partially massless response in the dual conformal field theory. As in the Einstein case, the holographic stress tensor of these instantons represents a perfect fluid with vorticity. Remarkably, we identify a non-Einstein Taub-Bolt branch supporting a nonvanishing partially massless response at zero source, while preserving the full symmetry of the squashed conformal boundary. The additional holographic degrees of freedom enrich the thermodynamic phase structure, allowing the conventional NUT/Bolt transition to disappear or give way to reentrant transitions. We further show that non-Einstein Bolts can possess negative thermodynamic volume and establish the absence of negative modes of a conformally coupled probe scalar on regular Bach-flat NUT backgrounds.

papers.title: Predictions of superconducting properties from chemical bonding interactions
papers.abstract: The need for rapid estimates of superconducting critical temperatures, Tc s, is becoming increasingly urgent as first-principles and artificial intelligence based methods enable the exploration of ever-larger and more chemically complex materials spaces. In this context, chemical bonding based quantities have emerged as promising descriptors for predicting superconductivity. To date, these approaches have mainly been developed for hydride superconductors, notably through the networking value, a descriptor based upon the electron localization function, whose topological properties have been found to correlate with Tc . In this perspective, we review and consolidate the method's theory, and we discuss how the estimate of the Tc is achievable within a real-space view. We conclude by proposing a framework that enables Tc prediction for the broad family of conventional superconductors from easily computable intermediate physical quantities.

papers.title: Insights on the mass composition of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays from small-scale anisotropy with large-scale structure simulations
papers.abstract: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) above 100 EeV provide important clues to the most energetic processes in the Universe. At the highest energies, it is expected that UHECRs originate only from nearby sources because of energy losses during propagation. In such a regime, small-scale anisotropies in arrival directions could appear if the magnetic deflections are sufficiently small, for example, for a limited fraction of UHECRs with relatively low electric charge. Using the Pierre Auger Observatory open data, we confirm there is no significant small-scale anisotropy above 100 EeV within 3 degrees, indicating an almost isotropic sky distribution. To interpret this, we consider that heavier nuclei have higher photodisintegration thresholds due to their smaller Lorentz factors, resulting in longer propagation lengths. Combination with the nearly homogeneous distribution of galaxies at such distances can explain the absence of anisotropies above 100 EeV. Based on this idea, we perform mock observations of UHECRs above 100 EeV assuming pure-proton, iron, and uranium compositions. We predict the expected UHECR distributions using the Millennium Run semi-analytic galaxy catalog and turbulent extragalactic magnetic fields. By varying the source density and magnetic field strength, we evaluate the anisotropy for each case. Without magnetic fields, the observed isotropy above 100 EeV excludes the pure-proton and pure-iron cases. The pure-uranium case can reproduce the observed isotropy when the source density is high and the magnetic field is turbulent. When the turbulent field is strong, both the iron and uranium cases remain consistent with the data, whereas almost no parameter set can explain the observation for a pure-proton composition. Our results constrain the possible combinations of source density and magnetic field strength across different UHECR compositions.

papers.title: Emergent Incompressibility in Polariton Condensates for Scalable XY Spin Simulation
papers.abstract: Driven-dissipative polariton networks offer a powerful analog platform for simulating continuous-spin Hamiltonians. However, their practical scalability is fundamentally limited by amplitude-phase coupling and metastable trapping in highly frustrated energy landscapes. Here, we present an \textit{in situ} dual-enhancement mechanism to address these bottlenecks without requiring external site-specific fine-tuning. First, a renormalization-group analysis based on density rescaling shows that higher-order nonlinear loss drives the condensates toward an incompressible regime, intrinsically suppressing amplitude fluctuations and enforcing phase-only dynamics. For macroscopic XY networks (up to 10,000 spins), this phase-amplitude decoupling yields a more than 50-fold reduction in energy, while simultaneously shrinking the standard deviation by a factor of six. More generally, it restores the extensive scaling of the optimized XY energy with system size. Second, to navigate the rugged, nonconvex energy landscape, we introduce weak Hermitian pulses. When implemented through a multistage protocol, these pulses enable repeated escapes from local minima and drive the system to deeper energy minima. Benchmarking shows an increasing advantage with system size, with the polariton simulator outperforming the classical Monte Carlo-SQP baseline in every sampled macroscopic realization. Our work provides a physical framework for scalable polariton analog computing.

papers.title: Timing is Everything: Inferring Temporal Membership in Continually Updated Models
papers.abstract: Continual model updating has become a common practice in the deployment of machine learning systems. However, the dynamic training behaviors give rise to new risks not sufficiently addressed by existing studies. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated deep learning models. We formalize the notion of temporal membership in continually updated models. We then define the temporal membership inference attack, which seeks to infer whether and when individual samples were involved in model training, at both timestamp-level and interval-level granularities. To this end, we propose TMIA, a novel black-box attack that leverages bidirectional LSTMs to infer temporal membership from model outputs observed across successive updates. Through extensive experiments on three language models and three image classification models, we show that TMIA is highly effective and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Finally, we evaluate three potential defenses, revealing the trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.

papers.title: Discovering like a scientist: Literature-informed dimensionless learning for physical closure of data-driven equations
papers.abstract: Data-driven methods can recover compact equations, yet the physical dependence of their coefficients across operating conditions often remains unresolved. Dimensionless groups can explain this variation, but selecting relevant groups from the many dimensionally admissible combinations remains challenging. Here, we introduce a knowledge-guided framework for dimensionless learning, called π-former. It learns patterns of variable association and exponent assignment from a corpus of 1,288 established dimensionless groups. Under exact dimensional constraints, the model proposes interpretable basic groups whose combinations are optimized against observations. Across seven physical problems, the framework identifies predictive dimensionless coordinates within seconds. Integration with equation discovery further expresses condition-dependent coefficients through these coordinates, recovering established physical scalings in multi-condition simulations. Applied to experimental measurements of evaporation-driven wetting, the framework discovers dimensionless coordinates and uses them to construct a unified trajectory equation. The resulting model generalizes to held-out conditions across liquids and initial volumes, outperforming existing empirical models. These results establish dimensionless learning as a transferable bridge between accumulated scientific knowledge and data-driven equation discovery, enabling artificial intelligence to uncover physically meaningful laws from observations.

papers.title: Private Vulnerability Testing for User Oversharing
papers.abstract: Users can inadvertently increase their vulnerability to privacy attacks by oversharing personal information. In particular, the combination of individually innocuous attributes can place a user in a sufficiently small population to enable linkage or re-identification attacks. We present a privacy-preserving mechanism that allows users to determine whether the information they disclose places them below a predefined population threshold, without revealing their query or the data of other users. Our setting presents several practical challenges: users contributing data may be offline when queries are made, queries may select arbitrary subsets of attributes, and neither server should learn the queried population or its size. We address these challenges using secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation. Our protocol provides computational privacy against a malicious client and semi-honest, non-colluding servers, while supporting arbitrary queries and dynamic database updates. We define reactive $f$-privacy for a dynamically evolving database and prove that our construction satisfies it, with the sequence of permitted threshold outputs defining the information available to the adversary across an execution. We optimise the protocol using oblivious-transfer extensions and pre-computation, achieving sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets of up to one million records.

papers.title: Coherence Spreading Law in Quenched Homogeneous Bose Gases
papers.abstract: We investigate nonequilibrium coherence spreading in quenched homogeneous bosonic gases both analytically and numerically. Our ensemble-averaged Gross-Pitaevskii trajectory approach and kinetic analysis confirm the linear-in-time growth of the squared coherence length, and explicitly give the spreading-law dependence on the ratio of initial energy to healing energy. When the ratio is relatively small, the squared coherence length grows at a universal rate determined by the ratio of Planck's constant to the particle mass, insensitive to interaction strength and initial momentum distributions. However, our further calculations uncover fundamental limitations to such universality and establish its phase boundaries governed by low system energies, weak interparticle interactions and many-body integrability. Our theory fully reproduces the key experimental signatures and resolves the puzzle of the dynamical origin of the recently observed universal coherence-spreading speed limit [Nature 647, 608-612 (2025)]. Going beyond existing experimental observations, we provide some testable predictions for ultracold-atom experiments and clarify the conditions for the emergence of universal coherent dynamics in nonequilibrium bosonic many-body systems.

papers.title: Optimizing Recourse Under Predictive Multiplicity
papers.abstract: Algorithmic recourse identifies modifications that can change an unfavorable model prediction into a favorable one. Under predictive multiplicity, similarly performing models can disagree on individual predictions, so recourse valid for one model may fail for another. We formulate robust recourse under predictive multiplicity as a budget-constrained minimization of the worst-case validity loss across a competing set of models, which can include models with different architectures or from different hypothesis classes. We propose an oracle-efficient algorithm called ORPM and prove sufficient conditions for its convergence. We evaluate ORPM on one synthetic and five real datasets, and competing sets consist of linear, neural, mixed, and decision-tree models. Our experiments show decreasing optimization-gap bounds and high validity in many tested settings, with favorable performance against baselines designed for specific model classes or architectures. We also quantify how requiring a common action across competing models changes recourse success at a given budget and examine disparities in this success across demographic groups.

papers.title: Exact teleportation bounds for fermionic Hawking thermality beyond the single-mode approximation
papers.abstract: Fermionic teleportation near a Schwarzschild horizon involves two physically distinct ingredients that are often varied together: Hawking thermal mixing and the relative composition of the right and left Unruh modes. We separate them by factorizing the reduced map of the detected exterior fermionic mode into a mode-preparation channel and a Hawking thermal channel. At fixed right-left Unruh-mode composition, we then solve a global constrained quantum-channel optimization over all two-qubit resource states whose fully entangled fraction remains at or below the standard teleportation threshold immediately before thermal mixing. A parity twirl and positivity reduce the arbitrary-state problem exactly to a two-variable quadratic optimization. The solution yields a necessary-and-sufficient activation boundary, a second exact boundary for attaining the universal optimum, and explicit optimizing states. The resulting phase diagram contains a strict no-go region, a composition-limited activation region, and a universal-bound region. The analysis converts state-specific observations of Hawking-assisted teleportation into exact channel-level bounds over the full two-qubit state space.

papers.title: Hotplug Coded Caching: Embedding the YMA and Interference Elimination Schemes via Reed--Muller Codes
papers.abstract: In the hotplug coded caching model, $K$ users fill their caches of size $M$ as a function of $N$ files, but only an unknown subset of $A<K$ users is active in the delivery phase. We recently showed that (i) under uncoded placement, offline users cause a strict load penalty at intermediate memory sizes, so that coded placement is needed; and (ii) for $AM\leq N$, every classical scheme with row-wise placement, including the scheme of Gomez-Vilardebo (GV), can be embedded in a Reed-Solomon code, which removes the penalty. In this note, we show that every point of the scheme of Yu, Maddah-Ali and Avestimehr (YMA) for a classical system with $A$ users is achievable in the hotplug model for every $K\geq A$. Each user is associated with a hyperplane and each file with a homogeneous polynomial; each user caches the restriction of the polynomial to its hyperplane, and the subfiles seen by the active users are the values of the polynomial at the points where their hyperplanes meet. This is a projective Reed-Muller code, which reduces to the Reed-Solomon code when each subfile is cached by one user. We then show, by an existence argument, that every classical scheme whose cache is a linear compression of the Maddah-Ali-Niesen cache and whose correctness holds for generic coefficients can also be embedded over a sufficiently large field; this includes the interference elimination (IE) schemes of Tian and Chen. These embeddings complement the Reed-Solomon one, which allows any row-wise placement and any delivery. Together with past work, our results show that every point attained by a GV, YMA or IE scheme ($N\leq A$ for IE), and every corner point of the linear tradeoff for $A=N=3$, is achievable in the hotplug model with a load that does not depend on $K$. Whether the optimal hotplug tradeoff depends only on $A$ remains open, but these results support a positive answer.

papers.title: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation
papers.abstract: This study investigates the authorship impersonation capacity of six widely used large language models (LLMs): Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.2 Pro, DeepSeek 3.2, and Grok 4.1 Fast. The evaluation was conducted using short product review texts selected to ensure high within author consistency in individual writing style. Two types of in context prompt were designed: a simple prompt with minimal instruction and a complex prompt incorporating explicit stylometric guidance for mimicry. Authorship mimicry was evaluated using a cosine distance based distance to training metric, supplemented by visual analyses of embedding distributions. The results indicate that authorship impersonation remained challenging for most LLMs, with Gemini 3 Pro showing the strongest apparent mimicry performance. However, subsequent overlap analysis revealed that Gemini 3 Pro extensively copied and reused sentences and phrases from the training texts, at levels far exceeding those observed among human authors. Follow up factor analyses showed that training set consistency was the most robust predictor of mimicry success across models, whereas author distinctiveness did not generalise as a reliable predictor. Global embedding visualisations further revealed a consistent macro level pattern: for most models, generated texts occupied regions of the embedding space that were largely separated from the corresponding human training clusters. This indicates limited convergence towards target author style and suggests the presence of model specific lexical and phraseological preferences. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing genuine stylistic imitation from direct textual reuse and have implications for the forensic analysis of textual evidence involving potential LLM enabled impersonation.

papers.title: Static and dynamical Casimir effects in a wedge within the worldline formulation
papers.abstract: We study a real massless scalar field in $d+1$ dimensions confined to a wedge of opening angle $α$, in the presence of a semitransparent circular arc that may oscillate radially. Within the worldline formulation, and for an arbitrary strength $λ$ of the $δ$-potential that models the arc, we expand the effective action in powers of the radial displacement $R$ of the arc. In this formulation, all the information about the media is contained in the propagator of a non-relativistic point particle, so that known results for that propagator can be used directly. At zeroth order we obtain the Casimir energy of the wedge, with Dirichlet, Neumann or mixed walls, and the contribution of the arc in closed form for arbitrary $λ$. We show that the worldline integrand is, point by point, the energy density obtained from the energy-momentum tensor of the scalar field with curvature coupling $ξ=1/4$; with this identification, and using dimensional regularization for the integrated quantities, we recover the known results for the wedge and for the wedge closed by a Dirichlet arc. At second order in $R$, we reduce the form factor that determines the imaginary part of the in-out effective action, and hence the probability of pair creation by the moving arc, to a one-loop expression involving the radial Green's functions of each angular sector. In the narrow-wedge limit, each angular sector behaves as a field with a mass set by the angular quantization, coupled to a moving $δ$-mirror; for a Dirichlet arc, the pair creation spectrum of the exterior region approaches that of a planar massive mirror, while the interior region behaves as a tapered cavity. Finally, by decomposing the electromagnetic field into TE and TM scalars, we obtain the Casimir energy of wedges with perfectly conducting, perfectly permeable and mixed walls.

papers.title: Priced In or Bet On? Cram-School Lessons, Jeonse Leases, and Expected Appreciation in Seoul
papers.abstract: South Korean families spend heavily on hagwons, private cram schools that prepare students for the university entrance exam. This paper asks what access to them is worth in housing and whether the premium includes expected appreciation. Using 2,197,510 Seoul apartment sales and jeonse (lump-sum deposit lease) contracts from 2015 to 2026, located with a new business-address geocoder, the analysis compares flats within the same middle-school assignment zone and month. Flats near hagwons preparing high-school students for the exam sell and lease for more: moving from the median complex to the 97th percentile of such hagwons within 500 meters is associated with sale prices 11.8% and jeonse deposits 7.3% higher, or 5.6% and 5.9% with complex size held fixed. Hagwons teaching younger children add no sale premium once these are held fixed. A larger premium in deposits than in prices across complexes reflects convenience: buyers pay less than renters to live near shops and services, above all repair and personal services. For the same flat type, complex and month, hagwon access produces no detectable change in the jeonse-to-price ratio, although the test detects the reconstruction value of old buildings; nearby shops raise it. Hagwon access is thus capitalized in proportion into prices and deposits, as expected of a current-flow amenity without extra expected appreciation. New tenants pay no lasting premium over renewing tenants, and deposits did not respond to major education-policy announcements. The housing premium is a cost of the education race that measures of tutoring spending omit.

papers.title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

papers.title: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete?
papers.abstract: Before an AI agent takes on a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed. We test whether frontier language models can make this call before any attempt. We propose PAYWORTHY which contains 1{,}494 real freelance job postings, sampled from 18.8M postings made between 2020 and 2026 on a freelancing platform. An agent attempts each job from the posting alone in a single run, and an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work. We ask 18 models to forecast how likely the agent is to succeed and measure how well each model's forecasts rank the accepted jobs above the rejected ones (AUC, where 0.5 is a random ranking). The answer depends on how the agent is described. Told what the agent cannot do, every model ranks the jobs well (AUC 0.66--0.86). Told instead that it is a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models rank the same jobs about as well as a random ordering (0.45--0.56). These results hold under judges from four other model families (Claude, GLM, Kimi and Qwen), and the informed forecasts also rank the verdicts of two human raters. Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Payworthy

papers.title: The most entangled states of four and seven qubits
papers.abstract: Pure states of four and seven qubits cannot be maximally entangled across every balanced bipartition; we determine how entangled they can be on average. For four qubits we prove the conjecture of Higuchi and Sudbery: the mean von Neumann entropy of the three $2|2$ cuts is at most $1+\tfrac12\log_2 3$ bits, with equality exactly on the local-unitary orbits of their state $M_4$ and its complex conjugate. For seven qubits the mean purity of the 35 balanced $3|4$ cuts is at least $121/917$ and their mean entropy is at most $2.965356029\ldots$ bits, each with a unique optimiser up to local unitaries and qubit permutations. The two optimisers are distinct members of one icosahedral family, so minimum purity and maximum entropy select different states. The proofs bound moments of the marginal spectra by positive identities on several copies of the state, some of them spin flipped, and bound the entropy by a polynomial in those moments. The four-qubit maximum has an analytic proof; the seven-qubit proofs, and some of the four-qubit refinements below, are computer-assisted, with exact arithmetic and rigorous error bounds. We also prove the Gour--Wallach conjecture for Rényi entropies of all orders, with the maximiser changing from $M_4$ to cluster states at $q_*\approx1.588$, and obtain sharp Tsallis bounds, mixed-state bounds and quantitative stability.

papers.title: Toward a Compositional Knowledge Architecture for a Shared Organizational Cortex
