In its first month of listing election contracts, Kalshi's prices were more accurate than every poll-based forecast in the national race, the seven battleground states, and nineteen Senate races, and no poll-based forecast would have been profitable to trade against them in any group of presidential contests. Its volume came from areas that voted 28% Republican, while 60% of volume went to Republican positions. Traders with a single trade placed 73% of their volume on Harris. The association between a trader's location and the direction of positions declines with trading activity and is zero among active traders, who account for most of the volume. Prices can be accurate with unrepresentative traders when the forecasts of profit-motivated traders do not depend on their demographics. Two other markets corroborate our findings. In New York's 1900 market, bettors were older than the population and drawn from finance. On PredictIt in 2016, which limited each trader to $850 per contract, positions followed registered party more closely, as our theory predicts when market restrictions do not allow profit-motivated traders to set the price. Prediction market efficiency is driven by financial incentives over demographic representativeness.

papers.title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

papers.title: Composite Variable Strategies for Continuous Endpoints
papers.abstract: Composite endpoints are common in clinical trials for binary, time-to-event or recurrent outcomes. Recently, there has been interest in estimands for continuous endpoints that employ a composite variable strategy for handling intercurrent events, whereby a value on the continuous scale is defined as the outcome. In this paper we describe these continuous composite endpoints where participants who experience the intercurrent event are assigned a pre-specified value on the outcome scale (which we call the failure value) instead of a measurement. We describe these endpoints and the difficulty of choosing the failure value when the mean is the chosen summary statistic. The large impact of the choice of failure value on the variance of the distribution of the endpoint is quantified as a function of the probability of the event and the standardised difference of the failure value from the mean of the unaffected values. Strategies for choosing failure values are discussed, emphasising the need to balance the clinical relevance and interpretability of the estimand with the need to reliably estimate it. Two potential solutions to situations where there is no relevant and viable choice of failure value are proposed; using failure values based on distributional characteristics to generate clinical relevance and using alternative summary measures to avoid the need to select specific values.

papers.title: Saturating $T^2$ resistivity in iron-based superconductors
papers.abstract: Many correlated metals exhibit a crossover from low-temperature $ρ\propto T^{2}$ behavior to a slower increase of the resistivity at elevated temperatures. Distinguishing phonon scattering from electron--electron correlations as the origin of this crossover is experimentally challenging. We introduce a simple phenomenological framework that isolates the contribution responsible for the high-temperature saturating tendency. This approach reveals a clear contrast between systems well known for the predominance of electron--phonon scattering and several iron-based superconductors. For the latter, the conductivity can be expressed as the sum of a Fermi-liquid-like term ($\propto 1/T^{2}$) and a temperature-independent component, which together describe $ρ(T)$ up to $\sim 250$ K in LiFeAs, KFe$_2$As$_2$, and KCaFe$_4$As$_4$. In FeSe, the same approach identifies a similar regime above the nematic transition, with a pronounced change toward nearly linear-in-$T$ resistivity below it. We discuss these findings in the broader context of coherence and electronic correlations in Hund's metals.

papers.title: Variable-Resolution Scattering Reveals Ensemble Properties
papers.abstract: SAXS/SANS determine the size and structure of particles and macromolecules in solution. However, the conventional low-angle determination of the radius of gyration, Rg, cannot separately resolve its scattering-weighted mean and the width of its distribution. Because the apparent Rg includes a contribution from ensemble variance, the distribution width is required even to recover the mean Rg. Here, we introduce TENOR-SAXS, a method for estimating the scattering-weighted width of an Rg distribution by applying two anisotropic digital smearings to a single 2D scattering image. Comparing the smeared images provides curvature information unavailable from the conventional radial profile. The resulting observables require no explicit model of the native instrumental point-spread function and show only weak sensitivity over the range of native resolutions typical of SAXS measurements examined here. Analytical expressions are derived in the low-angle and narrow-distribution limits for ensembles described by a known or independently constrained single-particle form factor. For verification, we simulated scattering by particles with several form factors and ensembles with different size distributions, all agree well with the analytical theory. To leading order, the principal observable depends on the scattering-weighted mean and variance rather than on the distribution's functional form or higher moments. For simulated data corresponding to feasible synchrotron exposure times for biological samples, the distribution width and, expressed as a fraction of its mean, was recovered with a typical discrepancy of ~0.1, while the scattering-weighted mean Rg was recovered with ~2% relative discrepancy. TENOR-SAXS thus provides a framework for estimating ensemble width from existing 2D scattering data without explicit instrumental desmearing and for correcting the variance contribution to the apparent radius

papers.title: Digital Nudge Effects in Optimal Stopping Games: Antagonistic Interactions in Layered Choice Architectures
papers.abstract: Digital nudges have become a prominent area of research in human-centered interaction, yet little is known about how they interact when deployed together. This study examines the individual and combined effects of anchoring, salience, and social proof digital nudges on stopping behavior and outcome quality in a sequential decision task. Using a 2^3 between-subjects factorial design grounded in the secretary problem (N = 181), we find that (1) an anchor nudge significantly increased exploration rather than constraining it (b = 1.207, p = .017); (2) the salience nudge produced the smallest effect of any condition; and (3) combining the anchor and social proof nudges produced the worst outcome quality of any condition ($181.83 vs. $192.21 for anchor-only), with outcome quality declining monotonically as nudge count increased. These findings provide the first controlled evidence for a digital nudge crowding-out effect with direct implications for the ethical design of digital interfaces.

papers.title: Occupational Uniqueness and Wage Growth
papers.abstract: Changes in occupational task content may have different economic implications depending on whether the tasks gained or lost are occupation-specific or already widespread across the economy. Existing measures of occupational task change largely abstract from this distinction, treating occupations as self-contained task bundles rather than accounting for how tasks are distributed across occupations. We develop a framework to measure a distinct dimension of occupational change, one that goes beyond task expertise or task content: task structure. Using this new framework that tracks tasks across occupations and over time, we separate changes in task quantity from changes in occupational uniqueness, defined as the distinctiveness of an occupation's task bundle relative to other occupations. Using a harmonized dataset of 196563 task statements from the Dictionary of Occupational Titles and O*NET spanning 1977-2018, we measure task diffusion, occupational uniqueness, and distinct dimensions of task addition and removal. Occupations that become less unique are also associated with lower wage growth, and the wage associations of task additions and removals depend on how widely the affected tasks are performed elsewhere. Adding highly diffused tasks is associated with lower wage growth, as is removing occupation-specific tasks. At the economy-wide dimension, however, the pattern differs: the addition of new tasks is positively associated with wage growth, whereas the removal of tasks is negatively associated with it. Taken together, these results show that similar changes in the number of tasks performed by an occupation can reflect economically distinct processes. Incorporating the cross-occupational distribution of tasks, therefore, provides a richer account of occupational change and its relationship to the wage structure.

papers.title: Speculative Imbalance Positions by Non-Physical Traders: Impacts on Electricity System Balancing in Great Britain
papers.abstract: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.

papers.title: Deterministic Causal Quantization with Bounded Error: Adaptive Reconstruction and Entropy bounds
papers.abstract: We study compression of real-valued stationary sources under a deterministic error bound: every sample must be reconstructed within a prescribed tolerance $\varepsilon$ on every input sequence. Reconstructions are causal, depending only on present and past inputs. Rates are measured by the entropy of the quantizer output, which block entropy coding can approach, and compared with the minimum rate of unrestricted block quantization under the same error constraint. A uniform scalar quantizer with cells of width $2\varepsilon$ is within one bit per sample of this minimum whenever finite-entropy scalar quantization is possible, without density, independence, or mixing assumptions. Under entropy and Sobolev regularity conditions, the gap is at most $2\mathcal{J}\varepsilon^2/(π^2\ln 2)$, where $\mathcal{J}$ is the asymptotic Fisher information per sample. Thus the cost of causal reconstruction vanishes at a quadratic rate as the tolerance decreases. A uniform grid, however, cannot adapt to the source. We construct an adaptive quantizer whose encoder and decoder maintain a common finite set of reconstruction values, updated from the transmitted symbols alone; suitable initialization reproduces any uniform grid. When its initial values are at least $\varepsilon$ apart, its rate is within two bits per sample of the minimum for every such source. For sources uniform within separated intervals of width $2\varepsilon$, storing the interval centers attains the minimum and its Shannon lower bound. Such configurations can outperform every uniform grid of the same cell width: over sources with well-separated intervals, the best uniform grid's worst-case excess rate is $1/(2\ln 2)\approx 0.72$ bit per sample.

papers.title: Quantifying the Threat: A Bayesian Probabilistic Framework for Heavy Metal Health Risks among Children in the Densu Basin, Ghana
papers.abstract: Groundwater in Ghana's Densu River Basin remains a key domestic water source, but multi-metal contamination threatens children's health. Previous deterministic hazard index assessments provide limited treatment of uncertainty, co-exposure, and spatial variability. This study applies a Bayesian probabilistic framework for non-carcinogenic risk assessment using 94 groundwater samples and measurements of Fe, Mn, Ni, Pb, Cd, and As. A Bayesian regression model propagates parameter uncertainty and accounts for contaminant co-occurrence. Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is used for posterior inference, while inverse distance weighting generates spatially continuous risk surfaces. Pb, As, and Cd dominate cumulative risk. Posterior predictive results indicate that approximately 31% of sampling sites have a probability greater than 0.5 of exceeding a hazard index (HI) of 1. The risk surface is highly heterogeneous, with a posterior mean of 0.372 and a standard deviation of 0.416. High-risk zones often reflect moderate co-exposure rather than extreme contamination by a single metal. The framework provides uncertainty-aware, spatially explicit information to support groundwater monitoring, risk mitigation, and public health planning in data-limited regions.

papers.title: System-evolutionary view of RNA presence in living cells
papers.abstract: Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA-DNA-Protein network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction-survival axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA-primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these have contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where RNA did not lose in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy and in its various forms has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.

papers.title: Cooling more while dissipating less: anomalous tradeoffs from thermodynamic geometry
papers.abstract: We show that, starting from the same state, optimal driving can sometimes reach a colder (or hotter) target in the same amount of time while dissipating less energy, or equivalently dissipate the same amount of energy in a shorter time. We study this counterintuitive phenomenon in the slow-driving regime of an open quantum system, where we name it Near-Equilibrium Anomalous Tradeoff (NEAT). We establish necessary conditions for its occurrence and show its underlying geometric origin. While NEAT is reminiscent of the well-known Mpemba effect, the two phenomena are distinct in general. We demonstrate NEAT in an exactly solvable qutrit model, as well as for d-dimensional birth-death dynamics with independently controlled energy levels. Finally, we show how NEAT can improve the performance of Carnot engines.

papers.title: Let Them Peek: Group Sequential Designs for A/B Testing
papers.abstract: Randomized controlled trials, commonly known as A/B tests, are the standard mechanism for inferring causal effects of product innovations. Standard platforms evaluate these tests with fixed-horizon procedures that control the false positive rate at a predetermined time, forcing teams to wait until the end even when early data strongly indicates success or failure. Unfortunately, continuous monitoring ("peeking") invalidates these guarantees, while always-valid inference is overly conservative under a strict deadline, and group sequential designs (GSD) have received limited traction in large-scale experimentation due to operational barriers: terminal-rule preservation, autocorrelation, latent effect-size distributions, calendar-duration optimization. We fill in this gap by proposing a Predictive Probability of Success (PPoS) group sequential framework that is autocorrelation-aware and duration-optimal while preserving the platform's fixed-horizon terminal rule. Our key insight is that PPoS thresholds map to closed-form lift boundaries that converge to the standard test at the horizon by construction, admit an effective-sample-size correction estimated from historical A/A tests, and suffice to attain the likelihood-ratio efficiency floor. Experimentally on online A/A and A/B experiments, we show that the proposed policy reduces expected duration by 43.1% (7.97 days vs. 14-day baseline), increasing effective platform capacity by 76%, while retaining the guarantees on FPR and power.

papers.title: Moments of Random Permanents and Hafnians: A Replica Approach
papers.abstract: Using contour-integral representations of the permanent and of the Hafnian, we turn the computation of their moments for random matrices into a replica calculation, analogous to that of the moments of the partition function of a mean-field spin glass. For the $2k$-th moment of $N\times N$ matrices with independent entries, the dominant saddle point is replica symmetric for $k>2$, and we obtain in closed form the exponential growth rate, the prefactor and the first $1/N$ correction, in agreement with exact enumerations. The growth rate depends only on whether the entries are real or complex; higher cumulants affect only the prefactor and the $1/N$ term. At $k=2$ the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law bulk of the distribution from a large-deviation tail, which we compute. The results apply to boson sampling with single photons and with squeezed light.

papers.title: Superconducting weak links at substrate steps in bilayer nickelate films
papers.abstract: Ambient-pressure superconductivity above 40 K has been realized in bilayer nickelate thin films on SrLaAlO$_4$ (001), yet resistive measurements often exhibit incomplete zero-resistance states and/or two-step superconducting transitions of unresolved origin. We show that these features arise from superconducting weak links at substrate step-terrace structures. A direct correlation between the azimuthal-angle-dependent two-step transition and step-terrace orientation establishes this connection, further supported by atomic-scale visualization of structurally disrupted regions at step terraces. Modeling the films as pristine (weak-link) regions with higher (lower) transition temperature reproduces essential features of the two-step transition using both a simple model and finite-element simulations. Transport measurements further reveal a strong dependence of transition characteristics - and even the occurrence of superconductivity itself - on average terrace width. These results identify step-induced weak links as the microscopic origin of two-step transitions in bilayer nickelate films, providing a framework for understanding anisotropic and percolative transport, and a route to superconducting devices.

papers.title: Non-uniform grids to accelerate electron-phonon coupling calculations for superconductivity
papers.abstract: Efficient and accurate evaluation of electron-phonon interactions is essential for predictive superconductivity calculations, but dense Brillouin zone sampling requirements pose a major computational bottleneck. To overcome this, we introduce an accelerated, highly scalable framework that combines a double delta truncation scheme with non-uniform Farey grids in both $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ space. The truncation strategy significantly reduces computational cost by restricting integration to states satisfying energy constraints near the Fermi level, while the Farey grids dynamically resolve sampling errors from localized scattering and stabilize convergence. Applied to elemental aluminium and several high-pressure hydrides, this combined methodology reduces computational cost by up to two orders of magnitude and yields electron-phonon coupling constants and superconducting critical temperatures Tc typically within about 5% of full-grid benchmarks. This approach overcomes sampling bottlenecks associated with dense uniform grids, making accurate, low-cost predictions of superconductivity in complex quantum materials feasible.

papers.title: Andreev Scattering Driven Surface Photogalvanic Effect
papers.abstract: The surface photogalvanic effect is a powerful tool for generating macroscopic direct currents in centrosymmetric film structures via asymmetric scattering of carriers at film boundaries. Here, we uncover a fundamentally distinct regime of photoinduced transport in normal metal-superconductor heterostructures, in which the macroscopic photocurrent is governed by Andreev scattering at the interface rather than by classical scattering. We demonstrate that the interplay between asymmetric surface scattering and Andreev retroreflection yields a giant, strongly frequency-dependent anomalous photocurrent. Strikingly, the electron-hole conversion at the normal-superconducting interface dictates a macroscopic sign reversal of the photogalvanic current across the superconducting transition, and induces non-analytic spectral kinks exactly at the pairing gap frequency. Our results establish the Andreev reflection-driven surface photogalvanic effect as a platform for optical control of superconducting correlations and suggest a direct, non-invasive spectroscopic probe for gap dynamics in hybrid quantum devices.

papers.title: Pressure-induced superconductivity in a bilayer metal
papers.abstract: We propose a model that explains the mechanism of pressure-induced superconductivity in a bilayer metal. Four types of pair potentials are assumed for a Cooper pair consisting of two electrons on different layers. Absence of local inversion symmetry gives rise to the spin-orbit coupling which is antisymmetric in the two layers. We assume that external pressure enhances the hybridization between the two layers. The stability of the superconducting states is well explained by the frequency symmetry of the induced pairing correlations by these potentials. Pressure-induced superconductivity emerges when the following two conditions are realized. (i) The spin-orbit coupling induces the odd-frequency pairing correlations and suppresses superconductivity at ambient pressure. (ii) The interplay between the spin-orbit coupling and the hybridization induces the additional pairing correlation that belongs to an even-frequency symmetry class. We briefly discuss the relevance of our model to real materials.

papers.title: BARRR: Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression for Multi-View Multi-Cohort Data
papers.abstract: Bidimensional data integration across multiple cohorts (i.e., sample groups) and views (i.e., sources or modalities) is crucial in biomedical research to derive holistic insights from heterogeneous datasets. However, most existing integrative methods focus on a single dimension, such as multi-view integration across distinct sources or multi-cohort integration across distinct sample groups. Existing approaches for bidimensional integration are scarce and predominantly unsupervised, overlooking the valuable insights offered by covariates. To address this gap, we introduce the Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression (baRRR) method. Our approach models covariate-related and unrelated effects concurrently, while also decomposing effect levels (global, partially shared, and individual) across both dimensions. Extensive simulations demonstrate the advantages of our method with respect to signal recovery, outcome prediction, and missing data imputation. We apply our approach to data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), using somatic mutations as covariates to inform patterns of variability across different omics platforms and cancer types. These studies highlight its potential as a robust and adaptable tool for integrative analysis in biomedical research.

papers.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $ε$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

papers.title: Who Gains When the Umpire Is a Machine? Evidence from the Automated Ball-Strike System (ABS)
papers.abstract: In 2024 the Korea Baseball Organization became the first top-tier league to replace the home-plate umpires ball-strike judgment with an automated system. Using over a million pitches from 2021 to 2026, we separate the change into the removal of human discretion and the imposition of a new zone geometry. The machine eliminated count-dependent calls, the value of catcher framing and a small advantage for star batters, rents worth only a few runs per player-season. Because the machines zone scales with height and treats every matchup alike, it redistributed strikes toward tall batters and across matchups, but few pitches are exposed to these changes, and their effects on plate-appearance outcomes are precisely estimated and close to zero. Pitchers re-optimized quickly by throwing higher, with left-handers catching up to an existing trend, whereas we find no evidence that batters adjusted. The results suggest that the incidence of replacing human judgment with a rule depends on its geometry and on exposure.

papers.title: Rashba-controlled emergence and reversal of critical-field anisotropy in p-wave magnet--superconductor hybrids
papers.abstract: We show that tuning Rashba spin-orbit coupling can change the in-plane field direction along which an $s$-wave superconductor is most susceptible to Zeeman depairing. We consider a two-dimensional $s$-wave superconductor subject to an odd-parity exchange field induced by a $p$-wave magnet. Without Rashba coupling, the out-of-plane exchange field enhances the in-plane critical field but leaves its angular response exactly isotropic, despite the anisotropic magnetic spin texture. Minimizing the Bogoliubov--de Gennes grand potential over uniform singlet pairing, we find that increasing Rashba coupling first generates and then reverses the principal-axis critical-field contrast, switching the minimum-critical-field direction by $90^{\circ}$. Equal principal-axis fields at the intervening compensation point coexist with residual angular modulation. We interpret the reversal through competing momentum-dependent depairing contributions from the magnetic and Rashba spin textures, while the on-site singlet pairing channel remains unchanged. Direction-dependent discontinuous collapses of the order parameter further shape the critical-field curves. These results identify a tunable directional paramagnetic response within the uniform-pairing sector. In heterostructures with sufficient electrostatic tunability of interfacial Rashba coupling, this reversal would enable gate control of the easy-depairing axis without reorienting the magnetic texture.

papers.title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas
papers.abstract: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.

papers.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
papers.abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings.

papers.title: Collective-Variable Stein Variational Gradient Descent for Free Energy Surface Exploration
papers.abstract: Enhanced-sampling methods enable molecular simulations to access configurational regions that are difficult to explore with conventional dynamics, but their efficiency often deteriorates as the number of collective variables (CVs) increases. Here, we introduce an enhanced-sampling framework that couples Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) with parallel restrained molecular dynamics simulations to facilitate exploration of higher-dimensional CV spaces. SVGD collectively transports an ensemble of interacting particles toward a target probability distribution by combining mean forces that guide particles toward low-free-energy regions with kernel-mediated repulsive interactions that maintain particle diversity. We validate the approach using an analytically solvable double-well model, followed by aqueous alanine dipeptide and tripeptide in two- and four-dimensional CV spaces, respectively. In each case, the particle ensemble reproduces the corresponding target distribution, and the reconstructed free-energy surfaces agree closely with analytical or umbrella-sampling references. For alanine dipeptide and tripeptide, CV-SVGD requires substantially less aggregate MD sampling than the corresponding umbrella-sampling reference calculations. These results demonstrate the potential of CV-SVGD as a flexible, parallelizable framework for enhanced sampling in multidimensional CV spaces. We additionally provide an open-source Python implementation to facilitate its adoption.

papers.title: A Bayesian machine learning approach to direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with noncompliance
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian machine learning approach for estimating direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with treatment noncompliance. To flexibly model outcomes and treatment receipt while accounting for within-cluster dependence, we combine Bayesian additive regression trees with cluster-level random effects. We augment the outcome regression with a peer-treatment clever covariate, defined as the predicted mean proportion of treated peers from a preliminary receipt model, to mitigate regularization-induced distortion of the effect decomposition. Within a Bayesian g-computation framework, we estimate cluster-average intent-to-treat effects and cluster-average local average treatment effects and examine sensitivity to the cross-world restrictions underlying their decomposition. Simulation studies show reduced bias under model misspecification, while the correctly specified parametric models show expected frequentist properties. We find that the clever covariate improves the decomposition of the total effect into direct and spillover components under moderate or strong spillover, with similar gains in smaller clusters. Its benefits vary with spillover strength, and the $95\%$ credible intervals remain conservative. An application to the Primary School Deworming Project in Kenya suggests reduced infection risk, with a larger estimated contribution from individual treatment receipt than from peer receipt. Overall, our approach provides a flexible Bayesian estimation of direct and spillover effect decomposition in the presence of treatment noncompliance.

papers.title: Learning the Geometry of Materials Space with Trained Neural Tangent Kernels
papers.abstract: Neural networks trained to predict materials properties learn representations whose physical content can be difficult to extract. We use the neural tangent kernel (NTK), evaluated at trained parameters, to recover the geometry learned by a network that predicts superconducting transition temperatures from elemental composition alone. Kernel ridge regression with the trained NTK closely reproduces the network's predictive performance and substantially outperforms regression with the initial kernel. Spectral analysis and multidimensional scaling reveal a geometry dominated by a small number of directions. Clustering and local neighborhood analysis organize compounds into recognizable superconducting families and connect materials with related chemical and correlated-electron properties despite substantial differences in $T_c$. These results establish trained tangent kernels as practical probes of learned materials representations, connecting property prediction with the exploration of materials space.

papers.title: Structural equation modelling--based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies
papers.abstract: Bivariate random-effects models are commonly used to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity in diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis. However, existing approaches may be sensitive to distributional assumptions and may produce biased estimates of accuracy and between-study heterogeneity with sparse meta-analytic data. We proposed a novel bivariate structural equation modelling (BSEM) approach for DTA meta-analysis and evaluated its performance relative to the bivariate linear mixed model (BLMM) and bivariate generalized linear mixed model (BGLMM). We conducted extensive simulations under varying study, sample-size, accuracy, and heterogeneity conditions. We assessed model performance using bias, root mean squared error (RMSE), confidence interval width, empirical 95% coverage probability (CP), and convergence. We generated study-specific random effects from bivariate normal, t, and Laplace distributions to assess robustness to distributional misspecification. We also applied the models to two empirical DTA datasets. The BSEM generally produced smaller bias and RMSE and nominal-level CP for pooled sensitivity and specificity than the BLMM, while the BGLMM generally yielded results between the two approaches. The BLMM showed stable convergence but tended to underestimate between-study heterogeneity. We observed similar performance patterns under the three random-effects distributions. In the empirical applications, differences between model estimates were generally consistent with patterns observed in the simulations. Overall, the proposed BSEM provided a flexible alternative approach for jointly modelling sensitivity and specificity in DTA meta-analysis, with performance that was generally favourable relative to the BLMM and comparable to the BGLMM across the simulated and empirical settings considered.

papers.title: Multifractality of human upper-limb velocity tracks motor optimization via hand dominance experiment
papers.abstract: Theoretical goal-directed movements follow a unique, stereotyped velocity profile, but continuous movement has no unique optimal solution, so it is unclear whether motor optimization makes continuous movement more stereotyped or more diverse. Previous studies indicated higher information content in the dominant hand, suggesting greater diversity. Because continuous velocity is a composition of overlapping joints movement of varying form, timing and amplitude, comparable to the events that compose spike trains and heartbeat series, we asked whether this diversity appears as a wider multifractal spectrum of velocity. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis to motion-capture velocity of cursive handwriting from right- and left-handed participants writing with both hands; hand dominance is a natural experiment in which task and geometry are fixed while optimization varies. With the dominant hand, spectra were wider, had a lower dominant exponent and were more positively asymmetric in both groups, whereas hands with the same functional role did not differ between groups. A logistic regression on the three spectral features identified the dominant hand with a cross-validated AUC of up to 0.93. Optimized continuous movement is thus not more stereotyped but more diverse: complex, neither stereotyped nor random, with multifractality that tracks hand dominance.

papers.title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
papers.abstract: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources - OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land - by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

papers.title: Determination of the Human-Robot Interaction Workspace for Robot Assisted Head Stabilization Control
papers.abstract: Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.

papers.title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
papers.abstract: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

papers.title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
papers.abstract: Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

papers.title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
papers.abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

papers.title: A latent control model for realistic rodent motion
papers.abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.

papers.title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
papers.abstract: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

papers.title: Regularization effects on the observational appearance of asymmetric thin-shell wormholes from a new string-cloud geometry
papers.abstract: We investigate how rational regularization of the new Letelier--Alencar string-cloud geometry changes the optical appearance of reflection-asymmetric thin-shell wormholes. We compare junctions with two nonregular exteriors, a regular observer exterior paired with a nonregular one, or two regular exteriors at fixed leading asymptotic masses, throat radius, string strength and regulator fractions. Critical scales, ray classes, orbit numbers and transfer functions are combined with three emission profiles and matched black-hole controls. Face-on and inclined images use the same prescribed emitter motion: circular timelike geodesics outside the innermost stable circular orbit and an inward plunge conserving its specific energy and angular momentum inside. Although the core is excised, regularization changes the retained exterior and throat matching. For the sampled parameters, the observer critical screen impact decreases from $10.392μ_1$ to $9.642μ_1$, where $μ_1$ is the observer-side asymptotic mass scale. Regularizing the second exterior then contracts the reflected interval from $3.890μ_1$ to $1.248μ_1$ without changing ordinary observer-side rays. Returned brightness depends on source support and velocity-dependent frequency shifts: the regular--regular image nearly coincides with its black-hole control for the outer-edge emission model face-on, while inner emission reveals returned structures. At large sampled inclination that near-degeneracy can be lifted. This separates regularization-dependent propagation from the emission and viewing conditions that determine its image contrast.

papers.title: Quantum algorithms for optimal control: large-scale finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulation
papers.abstract: We develop quantum algorithms for optimal control over a prescribed finite time interval (finite horizon), focusing on continuous-time linear-quadratic regulation (LQR). This foundational control problem often requires solving a nonlinear matrix Riccati equation, which can be costly for large systems and long control durations on conventional classical solvers. We instead work directly with the state-costate optimality equations, reformulating the LQR problem as a multiple-shooting linear system. Importantly, we prove a condition-number bound for the system that is independent of the horizon, under stabilizability and detectability assumptions. By incorporating the initial and final conditions into a single linear system, we can solve the subsequent linear system more efficiently with a quantum linear systems subroutine. For a given initial state, our quantum algorithms return classical estimates of the optimal cost and the optimal control inputs at a selected time, without constructing a Riccati solution operator. Given sparse-matrix block-encodings, an initial-state preparation oracle and a fixed number of control inputs, the query and gate complexities scale polylogarithmically with system size and control duration, provided that sparsity, relevant norms, and stability parameters are bounded. The dependence on the target error is inverse-linear up to logarithmic factors. We establish the required bounds uniformly in system size and duration for a family of damped mass-spring chains with two endpoint controls. Numerical experiments support the analysis.

papers.title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

papers.title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
papers.abstract: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

papers.title: Rational T cell repertoire allocation to control the gut microbiota
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota shapes host metabolism, development and immunity, yet how the host regulates its composition in the presence of complex ecological interactions remains poorly understood. Recent experiments that measured T cell reactivity to individual strains in germ-free mice inoculated with a defined microbial community found that T cell recognition across microbial strains is sparse but broad, with a few polyspecific clones recognizing antigens shared across taxonomically diverse strains. Reanalyzing these experiments, we show that these T cell responses are associated with abundance changes of the strains they target. To interpret these findings, we develop a model linking the T cell repertoire to microbial abundances, in which a repertoire is allocated to minimize microbe-driven harm at the cost of maintaining an immune response. The model rationalizes the observed sparsity of gut T cell reactivity and shows that this allocation can emerge from competition between T cells for microbe-derived antigens. Finally, we find that while immune recognition can regulate microbial abundances, ecological interactions between strains may interfere with this mechanism. Together, these results provide a quantitative framework for immune control of gut microbial composition and identify principles governing the organization of T cell repertoires in the gut.

papers.title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles
papers.abstract: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.

papers.title: A cross-cultural dataset on the structure of social networks: The ENDOW project
papers.abstract: We present multilayer social network data from 50 communities, located in 29 countries around the world, gathered as part of the "ENDOW" project. The communities show exceptional diversity, from fishers in Bangladesh and Vanuatu, to horticulturalists in Fiji and Bolivia, to pastoralists in Namibia and Argentina, to farmers and wage labourers in India and Colombia. Data collection embraced this variation, while still aiming for comparability. Respondents answered ten network prompts on behalf of their "sharing unit" (household), covering different types of material and immaterial support. From these, we construct networks representing flows of support between sharing units in each community. We compare nomination patterns and network summary statistics across the ENDOW communities and to other benchmark datasets. The summaries exhibit considerable heterogeneity, suggesting a need to revisit existing ``rules of thumb'' about social network structure. These measures contribute novel reference points for research on the diversity of human sociality and social structure.

papers.title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
papers.abstract: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

papers.title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
papers.abstract: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated eight models from three vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra; Gemini 3.8 Flash and 4 Argon) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for six of eight models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 4.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for seven models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, five models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin; one model also met the pre-set 30% limits of agreement, narrowly (-28% to +27%; limits outside 30% cannot be excluded), and the other seven did not. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

papers.title: QProtFuse: Query-Guided Layer Fusion for Retrieval-Augmented Protein Function Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting protein functions from amino acid sequences is essential to understanding biological processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible function descriptions to natural-language queries, yet their limited protein understanding motivates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing protein RAG methods primarily expand external retrieval signals while overlooking the rich knowledge encoded within a single protein language model (PLM). We show that retrieval performance varies across PLM layers and biological tasks, making conventional final-layer selection suboptimal. To this end, we propose QProtFuse, which uses queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein features and jointly learns protein and annotation retrieval through intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive objectives. On Prot-Inst-OOD, QProtFuse achieves the best protein and annotation retrieval scores, reaching 16.4\% Recall@1 with annotation reranking. These gains improve downstream RAG-based function descriptions, yielding the highest LLM-as-a-judge scores for both Qwen3-8B (6.22/10) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (6.68/10). Ablations and weight analyses demonstrate the value of query-guided fusion and complementary training objectives for exploiting a PLM's internal knowledge.

papers.title: Cassette-Editor: An Agent Harness for Editing Video the Way You Do
papers.abstract: Coding agents work in an environment built for them: a compiler or a test checks each change and points to the fault, and version control keeps every change in a project people can continue. Video editing agents lack one: an edit's correctness shows only in the costly rendered video, which does not point to the decision at fault, and existing systems offer either editing operations that cover only anticipated edits or a script whose output is a video the user cannot keep editing. We present Cassette-Editor, a complete agent harness for video editing that lets the agent edit the way a person does: knowing what the project allows, seeing what each change affects, and revising from there. The agent writes patches of typed changes to the editor's timeline document. A schema check and a rulebook shared with manual editing check each patch before it commits; a rejected patch leaves the project unchanged and returns each problem located with repair options, and an accepted one becomes a step of the history the user also edits. Reads map source analysis to the frames of the current edit. Because manual gestures are writes in the same language, folded by the same executor and rulebook, the agent can express every change a manual edit makes to the project. On 31 editing requests with the model held fixed, the complete harness passed 89% of trials against 47% for the same model with ten basic editing operations and without the rulebook, at less than half the agent time and cost per successful request; the loss fell on requests at rule boundaries, composite edits, and undo, not on finding content.

papers.title: Majorization for superpositions of nonorthogonal states and the existence of golden states
papers.abstract: Golden states, from which every state can be prepared by free operations, are the units of a resource theory. In the resource theory of superposition relative to linearly independent, nonorthogonal reference states, they were known only for two reference states and for special overlap matrices, all of them maximally coherent in the Löwdin basis. We determine what decides their existence and when this Löwdin pattern holds. For every overlap matrix, the robustness and the geometric measure of superposition are maximized by the same states, which overlap equally with all reference states; the maximal values are set by the ground-state energy of a classical $XY$ model on the dual basis. These states, and only these, are golden under the maximal superposition-free operations, but they need not be maximally coherent in the Löwdin basis. For the Kraus-type free operations, we prove Gram majorization, a necessary and sufficient criterion for converting pure states into targets with nonzero coefficients, which reduces to majorization for orthonormal reference states. It shows that every golden state of these operations is maximally coherent in the Löwdin basis, yet golden states exist only for special overlap matrices: three reference states that are not orthonormal admit one if and only if their overlaps have a common modulus $s$ and their Bargmann phase $Φ$ obeys $s\geq2\cos[(π+|Φ|)/3]$, so that a geometric phase decides whether the theory has a unit. Finally, equal-overlap states yield a complete family of superposition witnesses in the Löwdin basis, which show that white noise is a resource unless the reference states are orthonormal.

papers.title: Online Preplay and Offline Replay Optimize Action Selection in a Closed-Loop Navigation Model
papers.abstract: Hippocampal neurons not only encode the animal's current position, but also generate sequences representing potential future states and past locations. During goal-directed navigation, the represented location sweeps ahead of the animal's location (online forward replay). After such tasks, during rest, neuronal sequences occurring during sharp-wave ripples replay previously explored trajectories (offline forward replay). Following random foraging, however, neuronal sequences resemble Brownian motion, which does not correlate with behavior (diffusive replay). The mechanisms producing such diverse sequences, and their distinct effects on spatial coding and navigation, remain unclear. Here, we address these questions using a closed-loop model of navigation in a two-dimensional open-field environment based on a spiking neuronal network. In our framework, neuronal sequences are generated by a common mechanism driven by background noise and the balance of excitation and inhibition. Different replay modes arise solely from task-dependent synaptic modifications and serve different functions: online forward replay facilitates shortcut discovery, offline forward replay consolidates optimal sequences of actions, and diffusive replay helps in generalizing the action and state map and homogenizing internal connectivity. Together, these results show that a single network architecture can flexibly generate various replay types and clarify how each contributes to optimizing goal-directed navigation behavior.

papers.title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
papers.abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

papers.title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
papers.abstract: Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

papers.title: Time-Reversal Symmetry Breaking in the Centrosymmetric Nonsymmorphic Superconductor RuB2
papers.abstract: Centrosymmetric nonsymmorphic AB2 (A = Ru, Os) borides exhibit anomalous superconducting properties, but the microscopic nature of their superconducting ground state remains unresolved. Here, we investigate RuB2 using zero- and transverse-field muon spin relaxation (muSR), first-principles electronic-structure calculations, and Ginzburg-Landau symmetry analysis. Zero-field muSR reveals spontaneous internal magnetic fields below Tc = 1.6 K, providing direct evidence for time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB). Transverse-field measurements establish a fully gapped superconducting state, with a gap magnitude close to the BCS weak-coupling limit. Density-functional calculations show that RuB2 is a multiband Z2 topological metal with appreciable spin-orbit coupling. Guided by the experimental observations and the symmetry of the orthorhombic crystal structure, our Ginzburg-Landau analysis suggests that an internally antisymmetric, nonunitary spin-triplet state is a promising candidate for the superconducting order parameter. This candidate is consistent with both the observed TRSB and the fully gapped superconducting state. These results establish RuB2 as a promising platform for investigating unconventional superconductivity arising from the interplay of crystal symmetry, multiband electronic structure, and spin-orbit coupling, and motivate further studies of related nonsymmorphic borides. The two muSR measurements provide complementary constraints: zero-field data probe spontaneous magnetism associated with TRSB, while transverse-field data characterize superconducting field distribution and support a full gap. The topological electronic structure and spin-orbit coupling provide context for unconventional pairing. Although these results do not uniquely determine the order parameter, they narrow candidates and highlight that nonsymmorphic symmetry may shape superconductivity in RuB2.

papers.title: Gravitational Dark Matter Production in Einstein-Cartan Theory
papers.abstract: Introducing torsion into General Relativity leads to new four-point interactions for fermions. These are universal and must also affect any fermion dark matter. We improve existing calculations of dark matter production through the Einstein-Cartan theory four-fermion interaction by also considering the s-channel graviton exchange as another contributing process. The effect on both the total cross section as well as the momentum-dependent Boltzmann equation collision term is calculated and discussed. We also introduce the Holst term, which generally modifies the four-fermion interaction coupling constant as well as introduces two new four-fermion interactions, and discuss and compute its effect on the total produced dark matter abundance.

papers.title: Sidewall Metrology Protocol for Superconducting Qubit Devices
papers.abstract: Sidewall morphology is a potentially important factor influencing superconducting qubit performance, yet its quantitative characterization remains challenging due to the absence of standardized measurement protocols. In this work, we develop a scanning probe microscopy-based measurement framework for the quantitative characterization of superconducting qubit sidewalls. The framework introduces a refined root mean square lateral sidewall roughness descriptor and a new curvature-equivalent radius for quantifying vertical sidewall morphology. The descriptors and measurement procedures are applied to different components of qubit devices, forming the basis of a proposed sidewall characterization protocol. This provides a foundation for quantitative comparisons of fabrication processes across laboratories, enabling future investigations of correlations between sidewall geometry and qubit performance.

papers.title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity.
